name: anpilovml.ru
object_type: Portfolio — a single-page personal portfolio built as a job-application surface for a first ML/Python role. It is not a consulting site (no services, no rates, no client work), not a template repo (source is not published), and not an aggregator. The closest sub-genre is the 'entry-level ML engineer landing page': one hero claim (a hackathon win), a stack inventory, a project list, a process explainer, and a contact block.
format_genre: Scroll-page. A conventional vertical single-page scroll with anchor navigation across seven named sections, built as a Next.js App Router page with Tailwind utility classes. Two decorative sub-genre borrowings sit inside the scroll: (1) a 'Medical ML Dashboard' mock in the hero that renders a fake pipeline/telemetry panel (Medical Data -> NLP Features TF-IDF -> ML Model CatBoost -> FastAPI online -> Doctor Review, with a 'confidence 0.91 risk_case' readout and 'quality checks passed' badges), and (2) a small terminal pastiche near the bottom ('Мини-терминал состояния', prompt `~/anpilov/status`, one command `> whoami`). Both are presentational only — the dashboard is not connected to a model and the terminal takes no input. It is a scroll-page dressed in ML-product clothing, not a terminal-CLI or OS-simulation site.
intent_audience: Job-seeking, stated explicitly and narrowly. The contact section reads 'Открыт к стажировкам, Junior ML/Python позициям, проектам и задачам, где данные нужно превратить во что-то работающее' (open to internships, Junior ML/Python positions, and projects where data needs to be turned into something that works). Audience is Russian-market recruiters and hiring engineers: the meta description, keywords and OG tags all target the name + 'Junior ML Engineer' + 'VK Tech Hackathon' + 'портфолио'. There is no freelance framing (no pricing, no brief/spec intake, no 'order a project' CTA), no personal-brand play (no blog, no newsletter, no talks), and no gating. Secondary intent is narrative positioning rather than audience: the whole site argues one thesis — 'I do not leave the model in the notebook' — aimed at the standard junior-ML objection that candidates can train but not ship.
seniority_stage: Student / junior, and unusually candid about it. Self-labelled 'Junior ML Engineer / Python Developer' and 'начинающий ML-инженер' (beginning ML engineer). The About section volunteers the weakness directly: 'Коммерческого опыта пока немного, зато любопытства, практики и готовности разбираться — с запасом' (not much commercial experience yet, but plenty of curiosity, practice and willingness to dig in), and frames the portfolio as 'честное портфолио начинающего специалиста: без лишнего пафоса' (an honest beginner's portfolio, without excess pomp). The linked VK Tech post identifies his winning team as the 'Школа 21' team, i.e. he competed as a student of School 21 (Sber's peer-learning programming school in St Petersburg) [uncertain — the affiliation is inferable from the team name in the third-party post, and is never stated on the site itself; no university, no graduation year, and no dates of any kind appear on the site]. The corroborating GitHub account was created 2025-12-10 and has 5 repositories and 0 followers, consistent with roughly eight months of public output. For this item 'good' means legibility and credibility to a screening recruiter — clear role label, verifiable proof of the one strong claim, and evidence of shipping — not craft novelty.
language_i18n: Russian only. `<html lang="ru">`, `og:locale` = `ru_RU`, all prose, headings and CTAs in Russian. There is no EN/RU toggle and no `/en` route (probed: 404). The page is nonetheless heavily code-switched: every section label is an English kicker (About, Tech Stack, Projects, Highlights, How I Build, Interactive, Contact), several project titles are English or mixed ('OZON Recommendation System', 'Drone Strike / FPV Last Run', 'Commodity Dataset Builder', 'Agro Price Intelligence'), the entire ~60-item skills inventory is English technical vocabulary, and the footer line is pure English: 'Built with curiosity, Python and a suspicious amount of debugging.' Effect: an English-reading recruiter can extract role, stack and project names but not a single sentence of reasoning or the hackathon story. Given that the whole differentiating claim is expressed in Russian prose, the absence of an EN layer is the single cheapest missed improvement on the site.
url: http://anpilovml.ru — HTTP only. Port 443 actively refuses connections (ECONNREFUSED, not a timeout or a bad certificate), so `https://anpilovml.ru` fails outright even though the page's own `<link rel="canonical">`, `og:url` and `og:image` all declare the `https://` origin. Any visitor arriving from a source that upgrades or rewrites to HTTPS — an HSTS-primed browser, a link preview crawler, most social platforms, and Chrome's default HTTPS-First behaviour — reaches nothing. The self-declared canonical URL is therefore unreachable, which is a live correctness bug rather than a stylistic note.
owner_role: Dmitriy Anpilov (Дмитрий Анпилов) — Junior ML Engineer / Python Developer, Russia. GitHub bio: 'ML engineer in progress · Python · CatBoost/TF-IDF · Web apps · Building practical AI and full-stack projects'. Positions himself as a wide-profile builder rather than a pure modeller: 'Строю ML-пайплайны, backend-сервисы, Telegram-ботов, data engineering-системы и AI-помощников' (I build ML pipelines, backend services, Telegram bots, data-engineering systems and AI assistants), with the stated preference 'Люблю, когда модель не просто обучилась, а превратилась в работающий продукт с API, интерфейсом и понятной пользой' (I like it when a model hasn't just trained but has turned into a working product with an API, an interface and obvious usefulness). Headline credential: 1st place at the offline VK Tech hackathon in St Petersburg with an AI assistant for occupational-health physicians (врач-профпатолог).
sections_present: Seven anchored sections, all on one route (`#top`, `#about`, `#hackathon`, `#stack`, `#projects`, `#how`, plus the un-anchored interactive block, then `#contact`). Mapped to the standard checklist: About — YES ('Данные, код и рабочий запуск', a three-paragraph honest self-assessment plus three stat tiles: '1 место / VK Tech хакатон, Санкт-Петербург', 'Full flow / медицинские данные → ML → API', 'Wide stack / Python, web, mobile'). Projects — YES (7 entries, the largest section). Skills — YES, and unusually granular: a 'Tech Stack' section grouping roughly 60 technologies into 7 labelled clusters (ML/data science; backend/API; NLP & medical-domain specifics; MLOps/infra including model registry, model card, prediction logging, APScheduler; frontend TypeScript/Next.js/React/Tailwind; mobile Dart/Flutter/Flame/Riverpod; automation/Telegram bots/Git/Linux). Contact — YES. Experience — NO, and this is the most consequential gap: there is no employment history, no education entry, no dates anywhere on the page, and no timeline; the only temporal anchor on the whole site is the hackathon, and even that is undated on-site. Resume/CV — NO (no PDF, no inline CV; `/cv`, `/cv.pdf`, `/resume.pdf` all 404). Blog — NO. Three extra sections beyond the checklist carry most of the site's argument: a dedicated 'VK Tech Hackathon' section that promotes the single win to full-section status with the pipeline diagram and the external VK proof link; 'Highlights' ('Что уже есть' — nine bullets summarising what exists, honestly mixing achievements with capability claims and ending on 'Готовность быстро учиться' / readiness to learn fast); and 'How I Build' — a numbered 7-step method (01 parse the task; 02 prepare data; 03 train the model; 04 check quality — 'метрики, thresholds, ошибки и честный взгляд на ограничения'; 05 wrap in an API; 06 attach the product layer; 07 log, test and improve — 'Docker и спокойный запуск без ритуальных танцев'), which is the section doing the real work of answering 'can this junior ship?'.
nav_pattern: Single page, single route, anchor-based. A fixed header with the wordmark 'AnpilovML' and a `#top` link; `<html class="scroll-smooth">` supplies native smooth scrolling. Desktop shows inline anchor links; below the breakpoint they collapse behind a hamburger (`aria-label="Открыть меню"`). Two hero CTAs act as the primary nav for a first-time visitor: 'Смотреть проекты' (`#projects`) and 'Связаться' (`#contact`), alongside a direct GitHub link. There are no sub-pages of any kind, no per-project detail routes, and no breadcrumbs. Since the URL never changes, no section is separately linkable or shareable beyond the anchor fragments, and there is no sitemap.xml or robots.txt (both 404) to help a crawler discover structure.
visual_style: Dark technical minimalism in the 'AI startup landing page' idiom — the visual language of a model-serving product's marketing site, applied to a person. Composition is a stack of centred, generously spaced sections, each introduced by a small mint-coloured English kicker (About, Tech Stack, Projects…) above a large Russian headline, with content in translucent bordered cards (`border-white/10 bg-white/5`) over a near-black field. Design-trend alignment: glassmorphism-lite (the white/5 + white/10 hairline-border card recipe, used consistently for every card and every contact row) plus subtle depth effects that are named in the CSS — `tilt-card`, `light-field` (large blurred radial glows), `floating-shape`, `hero-parallax-layer`, `neural-map`, `neural-line`, `data-beam`, `scan-panel`, `winner-core`. Not a bento grid, not neo-brutalist, not kinetic typography, not a terminal site. The two signature bespoke elements are the hero 'Medical ML Dashboard' — a fake but domain-specific telemetry panel showing the actual pipeline of the winning project, which is a much stronger opening image than the usual abstract gradient — and the mint '1 / place' winner badge in the hackathon section. Notably, the site contains zero `` elements: every visual is inline SVG (68 of them) or CSS, including all iconography (lucide icon set, correctly marked `aria-hidden`). There is no photograph of the owner and no project screenshots at all — the site is entirely diagrammatic. This keeps it light and consistent but means a visitor never sees a single interface he actually built.
color_typography: Dark-only, committed at every level: `color-scheme: dark` on both `<meta name="color-scheme">` and `:root`, `<meta name="theme-color" content="#080A12">`, and no `prefers-color-scheme` query anywhere in the stylesheet — there is no light mode and no toggle. Palette: near-black background #080a12 with a secondary #081018, mint/spring-green primary accent #58F2C2 (a named Tailwind colour `mint`, used for kickers, the winner badge, links and hover borders), cyan #6EE7FF secondary, amber #FFD166 and violet #a78bfa as sparse tertiaries, and slate text (#e5e7eb body, #9ca3af muted). Typography is a two-font system loaded via `next/font` and self-hosted as four preloaded woff2 files: Inter for UI and prose, JetBrains Mono for code-adjacent and telemetry text (pipeline node labels, `~/anpilov/status`, tech tags), each with a generated fallback metric-matched face ('Inter Fallback', 'JetBrains Mono Fallback') so there is no layout shift on font swap. Type hierarchy is clean but heading-heavy — 1 `<h1>`, 8 `<h2>`, 22 `<h3>`. Contrast on the mint-on-near-black accent and the #e5e7eb-on-#080a12 body is comfortable; the #9ca3af muted grey on #080a12 is the weakest pairing and is used for a lot of the explanatory sub-copy.
motion: Moderate, ambient, and — unusually for this cohort — properly gated. Eight CSS keyframe animations drive everything: `ambient-shift` (slow background gradient drift), `particle-drift`, `gradient-pan`, `scan` (a sweep across the dashboard panels), `pulse-line` and `neural-dash` (animated pipeline/neural connectors, the signature effect), `caret-blink` (the mini-terminal cursor), and `spin-slow`. Section entrances use opacity + `translateY(28px)` reveals. Pointer-driven `tilt-card` hover tilt and `hero-parallax-layer` parallax add depth on desktop. Two levels of restraint are implemented in the stylesheet rather than left to chance. First, `@media (pointer: coarse)` flattens the experience for touch devices: `tilt-card` is reset to `translateZ(0)`, the blurred light fields are dimmed, and `data-beam`, `neural-line`, `scan-panel::before` and `winner-core::before` get `animation: none`. Second, `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` is honoured with a thorough global override — `animation-duration: .001ms !important`, `animation-iteration-count: 1 !important`, `transition-duration: .001ms !important`, `scroll-behavior: auto !important` on `*, ::before, ::after`, plus explicit neutralisation of the parallax, light-field, neural-map and tilt transforms. That combination (reduced-motion AND a coarse-pointer tier) is more than most portfolios in this set ship, and it is the site's clearest accessibility strength. Caveat: nothing on the page is animation-dependent for meaning, so the reduced-motion path loses no information — the gating is genuinely lossless. [uncertain — motion behaviour is read from the shipped stylesheet and markup rather than observed in a browser, because the origin was only reachable through a text-extraction proxy from this environment.]
responsiveness_mobile: Built responsive-first and the format degrades gracefully, because a scroll-page has almost nothing to degrade. `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` — correctly, it does NOT block pinch-zoom. Tailwind responsive variants are used throughout (42 `sm:`, 24 `lg:`, 11 `xl:`, 6 `md:`) against the default breakpoint set present in the compiled CSS (640/768/1024/1280px), so layouts reflow from single-column to multi-column at each tier. Navigation collapses to a labelled hamburger. The two format-specific risks are handled: the hero 'Medical ML Dashboard', which is the most horizontally complex element, is composed of stacked flex rows rather than a fixed-width canvas or a table, so it re-stacks rather than overflowing; and the coarse-pointer media query strips the hover-tilt and the heaviest ambient animations on touch devices, which also protects battery. The mini-terminal is a small fixed-height box, not a wide code listing, so it does not force horizontal scroll. The largest genuine mobile concern is not layout but the ~60-item Tech Stack section and the 7-step process list, which become a very long single-column scroll on a phone. Since the page ships no raster images at all, mobile payload is dominated by the JS bundle rather than media. [uncertain — assessed from markup, Tailwind variant usage and compiled breakpoints; not verified on a real device or emulator, as the origin could not be loaded in a browser from this environment.]
framework_hosting: Next.js App Router — unambiguous from the shipped artefacts: `/_next/static/chunks/webpack-*.js`, `main-app-*.js`, `app/page-*.js`, a `data-precedence="next"` stylesheet, `<meta name="next-size-adjust">`, React Server Component flight payloads pushed via `self.__next_f.push(...)`, and a build id `oSMTvjF-1SPf-bFmxZR_h`. Styling is Tailwind CSS (utility classes throughout, custom named colours `mint`/`cyan`, one compiled 29 KB stylesheet). Fonts are handled by `next/font` (four preloaded self-hosted woff2 files under `/_next/static/media/` with generated fallback faces). Metadata is generated through the Next.js Metadata API (canonical, OG, Twitter, keywords) and the OG image is produced by a Next.js `opengraph-image` route (`/opengraph-image?e05dbaa682be59b5`, which resolves 200). React version is 19-era (the flight payload references `react.fragment`/`react.suspense` sentinels). Hosting is the notable part: the domain resolves to 82.151.124.107, which RIPE attributes to PJSC Rostelecom (ROSTELECOM-MNT, MACROREGIONAL_CENTER, RU) — a Russian incumbent-ISP address block, not a managed platform. Combined with the fact that port 443 refuses connections outright while port 80 serves the site, this points to a self-managed origin (own VPS or a self-hosted box on a Rostelecom connection) with TLS simply never configured — the exact failure mode you do not get on Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages, all of which provision certificates automatically. There is no CDN fingerprint, no edge-cache header, and no platform header of any kind. Domain signal: `anpilovml.ru` — surname + specialism on the Russian ccTLD, cheap and readable, and a deliberate personal-brand choice (the same string is the wordmark 'AnpilovML'), but the .ru + HTTP-only + Rostelecom-IP combination reads as a hobby deployment rather than a production one. [uncertain — origin response headers could not be read from this environment; the deployment mode is inferred from the reachable-port pattern, the IP's RIPE attribution and the absence of any platform header in the served document, and it could not be determined whether the Next.js app is a static export or a running Node server.]
performance_a11y:
Performance: light in intent, unmeasured in fact. Positives are structural — zero `` elements (all 68 visuals are inline SVG or CSS, so no image weight and no layout shift from media), fonts self-hosted as preloaded woff2 with metric-matched fallbacks (no FOUT reflow), a single 29 KB compiled stylesheet, and Next.js code splitting with four async chunks. The offsetting costs are the React/Next.js client runtime for a page that is mostly static text, and the ambient animation set (blurred light fields, parallax layers, pulsing connectors) which is compositor work on every frame — though this is explicitly downgraded on coarse-pointer devices. The much larger real-world performance fact is not bytes but reachability: the origin is on a Rostelecom consumer/business IP with no CDN, so latency and availability depend on one Russian home-region host, and it was intermittently unreachable during research. Accessibility: better than most sites in this cohort, with clear gaps. Present and correct — `lang="ru"`; a single `

` with a sensible `h2`/`h3` descent; 71 `aria-*` attributes with all 68 decorative SVGs marked `aria-hidden="true"`; real `aria-label`s on the interactive controls that need them ('Открыть меню', 'Скопировать Email', 'Скопировать Telegram', 'Скопировать Телефон'); a viewport that permits zoom; a full `prefers-reduced-motion` implementation; and — importantly — all substantive content is real server-rendered text in the HTML document, so a screen reader and a crawler both get the whole portfolio without executing anything. analytics_instrumentation: None. No Google Analytics or gtag, no Google Tag Manager, no Yandex.Metrica (`mc.yandex` absent — notable for a Russian-market site, where Metrica is the default choice), no VK retargeting pixel, no Plausible, no Umami, no Fathom, no Vercel Analytics, no Microsoft Clarity, and no session-replay tooling. The only occurrences of the string 'yandex' in the document are the owner's own `@yandex.ru` email address. There is correspondingly no cookie or consent banner, which is consistent — nothing is being set. The owner therefore has no data on whether the site is being visited, which sections are read, or how often the contact copy-buttons are used; for a job-seeking site whose conversion event is an outbound Telegram or email message, that is a defensible omission rather than a mistake, though it also means the HTTPS-refusal bug would produce no visible signal.
project_presentation: Seven projects in a single 'Projects' section under the thesis headline 'Проекты, где модель не остаётся в ноутбуке' (projects where the model doesn't stay in the notebook). Each is a uniform card with four consistent parts: a category tag, a title, a prose description of 1–3 sentences, a witty one-line aside, and a row of technology tags. The set, in order: (1) 'AI-помощник врача-профпатолога' [ML / Backend] — the hackathon winner, described with genuine technical specificity: medical texts, ICD (МКБ) codes, harmful-factor data, TF-IDF, CatBoost, an ensemble approach, threshold tuning and quality checks; tags Python, Pandas, Scikit-learn, CatBoost, TF-IDF, NLP medical text processing, FastAPI, pytest, MLOps basics. (2) 'OZON Recommendation System' [ML] — next-purchase prediction; feature engineering, model training, evaluation and approach comparison; LightGBM/Scikit-learn/Jupyter. (3) 'Drone Strike / FPV Last Run' [Mobile / Backend] — a 2D FPV-drone arcade game; Flutter/Flame client with game loop, obstacles, missions, lives, music/SFX, plus a FastAPI backend with profiles, progress and a leaderboard. (4) 'Commodity Dataset Builder' [Backend / Automation] — a long-lived data-engineering system for collecting and normalising commodity market data, explicitly citing immutable raw storage, a scheduler, health reports and Alembic migrations. (5) 'Сайт управления муниципального заказа' [Web] — a Next.js public site plus CMS plus internal procurement/request tracking. (6) 'Telegram Price Monitor Bot' [Automation] — price monitoring for oils and meals with manual and scheduled collection, price history, digests, 7-day charts and notifications; described as part of the Agro Price Intelligence system. (7) 'Agro Price Intelligence' [Data Engineering / ML / Agriculture] — the umbrella system: parsing industry and exchange sources, Telegram notifications, price history storage, charts, and dataset preparation for a future forecasting model, with the goal stated openly as building a quality historical base first. Strengths of the presentation: the taxonomy tags do real work (ML, Mobile, Web, Automation, Data Engineering) and demonstrate breadth honestly; the descriptions name specific techniques rather than buzzwords; the collection tells a coherent story (two of the seven are deliberately framed as one in-progress agro-data programme, which reads as sustained effort rather than a pile of tutorials); and one project carries a genuine scope-and-ethics caveat ('Не заменяет врача — помогает подсветить рисковые случаи'). The decisive weakness: LIVE-DEMO AVAILABILITY IS ZERO AND SO IS CODE AVAILABILITY. A complete extraction of every `href` on the page yields exactly six external destinations — one GitHub profile link, one Telegram link, one VK post, a mailto, a tel, and the site's own canonical. Not one project card links to a repository, a deployed demo, a Hugging Face Space, a Vercel URL, a notebook, a model card, or a screenshot. There is no per-project detail page. Since the site ships no `` at all, a visitor cannot even see a picture of any of the seven. Everything therefore rests on the reader's willingness to believe unillustrated prose — which is precisely the wrong bet for a junior candidate whose central problem is credibility. The gap is self-inflicted rather than unavoidable: the owner's public GitHub does contain a relevant `hackathon` repo (Python, topics catboost/nlp/tf-idf/medical-ai/classification, pushed 2026-05-31) plus `telegramm_bot_price`, `long_play_project` and `ochag`, and the site links to none of them individually.
resume_integration_mode: None of the four modes. There is no PDF download, no inline HTML CV, no ATS-parseable structured resume, and no link to hh.ru, LinkedIn, Habr Career or any CV host — `/cv`, `/cv.pdf` and `/resume.pdf` all return 404. What a parser would extract from the page is real and reasonably rich (name, role label, ~60 technologies, 7 project descriptions, contact details, all present as server-rendered text), but it is missing every field a resume screen actually keys on: no employer, no job title history, no education institution, no dates or durations of any kind, and no location beyond the hackathon city. The practical consequence is that this site cannot substitute for a CV in a Russian-market application flow — it can only supplement one — and because no CV is linked, a recruiter who lands here has no route to the machine-readable version. For a site whose sole purpose is job-seeking, the absence of both a downloadable CV and any dated experience is the largest content gap on the page.
proof_verifiability: Strong on the one claim that matters, and absent everywhere else — an unusually barbelled profile. THE HACKATHON WIN IS PROPERLY CITED AND INDEPENDENTLY CHECKS OUT. The site links from its dedicated hackathon section to a specific third-party post (vk.com/wall-187903410_8503, the VK page of the 'Мой медицинский центр' group of companies), and that post confirms the substance: on 16–17 May 2026 VK Tech and the MMC group ran a joint offline hackathon in St Petersburg in which 8 student teams from ITMO, SPbETU 'LETI', SPbSUT, School 21, SPbU and others built a prototype AI model for occupational-health physicians; it lists first place going to two teams, one of which is the 'Школа 21' team comprising Дмитрий Анпилов, Семён Боровской and Татьяна Четверикова. The event is further corroborated by independent coverage (dp.ru, 18 May 2026, and an ETU/LETI university news item), which matches the dates, city, organisers and subject matter. This is a materially better proof pattern than the norm: a named third-party source, linked directly, rather than an unlinked badge or an assertion. Two honest caveats surface only from the external source, not from the site: first place was SHARED with a second team ('Егетлар'), and the win was a three-person team effort — the site says 'Проект... занял 1 место' and never names the teammates or clarifies his own contribution, so a reader could reasonably infer more solo ownership than the record supports. That is an omission rather than a misstatement, but naming the two teammates would cost one line and would read as more credible, not less. EVERYTHING ELSE IS UNVERIFIABLE BY CONSTRUCTION. The other six projects have no repository link, no demo, no screenshot and no detail page, so claims like 'immutable raw storage, scheduler, health reports and Alembic migrations' or a FastAPI leaderboard backend cannot be checked at all. The ~60-item Tech Stack inventory — which includes weighty MLOps claims such as model registry, model card, prediction logging and data validation — is a flat unsourced list; nothing on the page or in the public GitHub demonstrates a model registry or a model card. The hero dashboard displays a 'confidence 0.91 risk_case' figure with no methodology, dataset or context, which is decorative telemetry presented in the visual grammar of a real metric. And a small consistency tell in the contact block: two GitHub cards sit side by side, one labelled 'DimaUMZ' and one labelled 'dmitriyrabota90-svg', but both link to the same `github.com/dmitriyrabota90-svg` profile — while `github.com/DimaUMZ` exists as a separate real account [uncertain — most likely a leftover from a handle change or a copy-paste error in the contact data, but the intent cannot be determined from the page]. Net: the site proves its headline exactly the way it should, then fails to apply the same standard to anything else.
quantified_impact: Almost none, and the little that appears is unanchored. The genuine quantities on the page are competitive rather than outcome-based: '1 место' (first place), rendered as a large '1 / place' badge, and the count of 8 competing teams — the latter available only in the linked VK post, not on the site. Beyond that: seven projects, roughly 60 listed technologies, a 7-step build process, '7 дней' as the window for the Telegram bot's price charts. There is not one model metric — no ROC-AUC, F1, precision/recall, PR-AUC or accuracy for the CatBoost/TF-IDF ensemble, despite the hackathon having been judged partly on automatic-leaderboard position and model quality, which means a real number exists and simply was not published. No latency or throughput figures for any FastAPI service. No dataset sizes, no row or record counts for the commodity/agro data collection (the one project where volume would be the natural proof). No user counts for the Telegram bot or the Flutter game. No cost, time-saved or workload-reduction estimate for the medical assistant, even though the linked VK post supplies exactly that framing from the client side ('снизить рутинную нагрузку на специалистов'). The only numeral that looks like a metric — 'confidence 0.91 risk_case' in the hero dashboard mock — is presentational, attached to no evaluation protocol or dataset, and is arguably worse than no number at all because it borrows the authority of measurement without the substance. For a candidate whose whole pitch is 'I check quality honestly — метрики, thresholds, ошибки и честный взгляд на ограничения' (step 04 of How I Build), the absence of a single published metric is the sharpest internal contradiction on the site.
content_freshness: Recent but undated, which wastes most of the recency it actually has. The site itself contains no date, no 'last updated', no changelog, no 'currently working on' widget and no copyright year — a visitor cannot tell from the page whether it was built last month or two years ago. External signals show it is genuinely current: the hackathon it centres on took place 16–17 May 2026 (two and a half months before research), the supporting GitHub account was created 2025-12-10 and was last active 2026-07-21, and the `hackathon` repo was pushed 2026-05-31. The nearest thing to a forward-looking status indicator is content rather than metadata: the Agro Price Intelligence entry is explicitly framed as work in progress toward a future forecasting model ('подготовка датасета для будущей ML-модели', 'Цель — собрать качественную историческую базу данных'), and the About section calls out that data programme as a separate ongoing direction — so the site does communicate an active trajectory, just not a timestamp. Two staleness risks are worth noting: nothing on the page will visibly age, so it will read as equally fresh in a year unless edited; and because the hackathon is the sole temporal anchor and is undated on-site, the strongest claim loses value over time in a way the owner will not be prompted to fix.
writing_tone: First-person Russian, plain-spoken, self-deprecating and consistently well-judged — the strongest asset on the site and the thing most worth copying. Three registers are held in balance. (1) DISARMING HONESTY, deployed early rather than buried: 'Честное портфолио начинающего специалиста: без лишнего пафоса, зато с реальными сборками, экспериментами и руками в коде', and then the concession most juniors hide — 'Коммерческого опыта пока немного, зато любопытства, практики и готовности разбираться — с запасом'. Rather than reading as weakness, this buys credibility for the claims that follow. (2) ENGINEERING PRAGMATISM as the through-line: the site repeatedly argues process over hype — 'улучшаю без магического мышления' (I improve without magical thinking), 'честный взгляд на ограничения' (an honest look at limitations), 'спокойный запуск без ритуальных танцев' (a calm launch without ritual dancing), and the section headline 'Проекты, где модель не остаётся в ноутбуке'. This is precisely the vocabulary that distinguishes someone who has shipped from someone who has only trained. (3) DRY HUMOUR, one line per project, never at the expense of clarity: 'Модель умная, но халат не носит' (the model is smart but doesn't wear a lab coat) on the medical assistant; 'Покупка ещё не сделана, а признаки уже нервничают' (the purchase hasn't happened yet but the features are already nervous) on the recommender; 'Данные приходят регулярно, складываются аккуратно и не спорят с миграциями' on the dataset builder; 'Когда ML-модель устала — можно отправить FPV-дрон в миссию'; 'Госзаказ, но интерфейс старается быть человеком' (a government order, but the interface tries to be a human); and the English footer, 'Built with curiosity, Python and a suspicious amount of debugging.' The interactive block extends the joke with 'кофе как критической зависимостью' (coffee as a critical dependency). Crucially, the humour sits in a separate slot from the technical description, so the substance is never diluted — a pattern any portfolio can adopt. The one place the voice oversteps is the medical project's ethical caveat, which is correct and admirable but shares a line with a joke; and the tone cannot rescue the structural problem that these well-written claims have nothing linked behind them.
standout_features: Ranked by borrowability for a conventional software-engineer portfolio. CHEAP AND WORTH STEALING: 1. PROMOTE ONE VERIFIABLE WIN TO ITS OWN FULL SECTION, WITH THE THIRD-PARTY LINK IN IT. The hackathon gets a dedicated `#hackathon` section — badge, one-paragraph explanation of what the system does, the pipeline diagram, and a direct link to the organiser's own post. This is the single best-executed idea on the site: instead of a bullet claiming a win, there is a citation. Almost free to copy, and it converts the strongest claim from assertion into evidence. 2. THE 'HOW I BUILD' 7-STEP SECTION. A numbered, plainly-written method (parse the task → prepare data → train → check quality → wrap in an API → attach the product layer → log/test/improve) that pre-empts the exact objection a junior faces: 'can you actually ship?' It costs seven short paragraphs and no engineering, and it does more persuasive work than any animation on the page. This generalises to any discipline — a backend engineer's or a frontend engineer's version of the same section would be equally effective. 3. A DOMAIN-SPECIFIC HERO DIAGRAM INSTEAD OF AN ABSTRACT GRADIENT. The hero renders the actual architecture of the flagship project (Medical Data → TF-IDF → CatBoost → FastAPI → Doctor Review) in HTML/CSS/SVG. It tells a visitor what the person does within two seconds, weighs nothing, and needs no screenshots — a strong pattern for anyone whose work is a pipeline or a system rather than a UI. Caveat: keep the fake telemetry numbers out of it (see #10). 4. GROUPED, LABELLED TECH STACK RATHER THAN ONE FLAT TAG CLOUD. Seven clusters (ML/data; backend/API; domain NLP; MLOps/infra; frontend; mobile; automation/tooling) make ~60 technologies scannable and make breadth legible as structure rather than as noise. 5. HONEST-LIMITATION LINES. 'Не заменяет врача — помогает подсветить рисковые случаи' on a medical ML project, and 'Коммерческого опыта пока немного' in the About. Volunteering the boundary of your own work is a credibility multiplier and costs one sentence. 6. ONE-LINE HUMOUR SLOT PER PROJECT, kept strictly separate from the technical description. Differentiates the voice with zero cost to clarity — a reusable content pattern, not a design one. 7. COPY-TO-CLIPBOARD BUTTONS ON EVERY CONTACT ROW, each with a real `aria-label` ('Скопировать Email' etc.). Tiny, genuinely useful, and correctly labelled. 8. A CONSISTENT ENGLISH KICKER ABOVE EVERY RUSSIAN HEADLINE (About, Tech Stack, Projects, Highlights, How I Build, Contact). A cheap bilingual affordance that lets a non-Russian reader navigate the page structure — though it also highlights how much more value a real EN toggle would add. 9. AN ALL-SVG, ZERO-IMAGE BUILD. 68 inline SVGs and no `` at all: no image weight, no layout shift, no asset pipeline, and consistent theming. Worth borrowing as a discipline for diagrammatic sites — with the strong caveat in the anti-pattern list below. GENUINE TECHNICAL RESTRAINT WORTH NOTING: 10. A TWO-TIER MOTION DOWNGRADE — `@media (pointer: coarse)` strips hover-tilt and the heaviest ambient animations for touch devices, and a thorough `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block neutralises animations, transitions, smooth scrolling and the parallax/tilt transforms. Because no content is animation-dependent, the reduced path is lossless. This is more motion hygiene than most portfolios in this set ship, and it is entirely CSS. ANTI-PATTERNS — THE INSTRUCTIVE PART OF THIS ITEM: 11. ZERO LINKS ON SEVEN PROJECT CARDS. No repos, no demos, no screenshots, no detail pages — while a relevant public `hackathon` repository (with matching CatBoost/TF-IDF/medical-AI topics) sits one click away on the owner's GitHub, unlinked. A junior portfolio's entire job is converting claims into checkable artefacts; this site does that once, brilliantly, and then not at all. Fixing it requires no design work. 12. FAKE METRICS IN REAL-METRIC CLOTHING. 'confidence 0.91 risk_case' and 'quality checks passed' are decorative, yet rendered in the visual language of live telemetry. A reader who realises they are mock loses trust in the numbers that ARE real. Either wire it to something or drop the digits. 13. A DECLARED HTTPS CANONICAL ON AN HTTP-ONLY ORIGIN. ``, `og:url` and `og:image` all point at an origin that actively refuses port 443, so link previews, HTTPS-First browsers and many crawlers get nothing. The most severe defect on the site, and purely operational. 14. NO DATES AND NO CV ANYWHERE on a site whose sole purpose is job-seeking — no employment or education history, no timeline, no downloadable resume, and no link to an external CV, so a recruiter has no route to the machine-readable version. 15. NO FOCUS-VISIBLE STYLING at all, on a dark translucent-card design where default focus rings are hardest to see — an odd blind spot on a site that otherwise handles reduced motion carefully. STRUCTURAL LESSON: this site is a near-perfect illustration of the junior-portfolio trade-off. Its writing, its process section and its single citation are genuinely better than most senior portfolios; its evidence layer is empty. The transferable insight is that the highest-ROI work on an early-career portfolio is not visual — it is linking artefacts and publishing numbers, both of which this owner already has and simply did not surface.
originality_vs_template: Custom build with no identifiable template lineage — no starter-kit fingerprints (no `next-themes`, no shadcn/ui component signatures, no Aceternity/Magic UI class names, no portfolio-template attribution comment or footer credit), and the bespoke elements are clearly hand-authored: the semantic CSS class vocabulary (`winner-core`, `neural-map`, `data-beam`, `scan-panel`, `light-field`, `tilt-card`), the project-specific hero pipeline diagram, and the 7-cluster stack taxonomy. That said, it is firmly inside a well-worn GENRE rather than outside it: dark near-black background, single mint/cyan accent on translucent `white/5` cards with `white/10` hairline borders, Inter + JetBrains Mono, small English kicker above a large headline, ambient blurred glows — this is the default Next.js + Tailwind 'AI product landing page' aesthetic, and the palette and card recipe would be recognisable to anyone who has seen a dozen 2025–2026 developer portfolios. So: original in code and content, conventional in look. The convention is arguably the right call for a job-seeking junior — legibility beats novelty for a recruiter audience — but it means the site's differentiation is carried entirely by its writing and its one citation, not by its design.
source_available: No. The site's own repository is not published: the owner's GitHub account (`dmitriyrabota90-svg`) holds 5 public repositories — `long_play_project` (Python), the `dmitriyrabota90-svg` profile README, `hackathon` (Python), `ochag` (Dart), and `telegramm_bot_price` (Python) — and none is the Next.js portfolio, nor is there any link, `humans.txt`, or footer credit pointing to source. So there is no self-dogfooding signal from the site itself. The related and more damaging point is that the repositories that DO exist are never linked from the projects they correspond to: `hackathon` is exactly the flagship medical-ML project (description: 'AI assistant for occupational health screening using classical ML, TF-IDF text features, CatBoost and validation logic'; topics catboost, classification, machine-learning, medical-ai, nlp, python, tf-idf; created 2026-05-22, pushed 2026-05-31, ~11 MB, no licence), and `telegramm_bot_price` maps to the Telegram Price Monitor Bot — both reachable only by manually browsing the profile link in the contact section. Three of the seven site projects (OZON Recommendation System, the municipal-procurement Next.js site, Agro Price Intelligence as an integrated system) have no corresponding public repository at all. None of the five repos carries a licence.
contact_methods: One dedicated `#contact` section at the end of the page, opened by an explicit availability statement ('Открыт к стажировкам, Junior ML/Python позициям...'), plus a GitHub link in the hero CTA row. Four channels, each presented as a translucent card with the value shown in full as visible text and a copy-to-clipboard button beside it (six copy affordances in total, labelled 'Скопировать Email', 'Скопировать Telegram', 'Скопировать Телефон'): GitHub (`github.com/dmitriyrabota90-svg`, shown twice — once labelled 'DimaUMZ' and once labelled with the actual handle, both pointing at the same profile); Telegram (`@AnpilovDmitriy` → `t.me/AnpilovDmitriy`); phone (`+7 960 636-36-63`, a live `tel:` link); and email (`anpilovdmitriy@yandex.ru`, a live `mailto:`). There is no contact form, no scheduling link, no LinkedIn, no hh.ru or Habr Career profile, no VK personal page, and no Kaggle or Hugging Face profile — a notable omission for an ML candidate, since Kaggle/HF would double as portfolio evidence. Placement is end-of-page only: apart from the hero GitHub button there is no persistent header or footer contact affordance, so reaching out requires scrolling the full length of the page. Channel mix is well matched to the Russian market (Telegram-first, Yandex mail, phone), and showing each value as selectable text rather than hiding it behind an icon is the right call for a recruiter who wants to copy it into an ATS.
pii_exposure: The highest PII exposure of any site in this set, and deliberate rather than accidental. Exposed in cleartext, as visible text AND as live links AND with copy-to-clipboard helpers: a personal mobile phone number, +7 960 636-36-63, behind a `tel:` link; and a personal email, anpilovdmitriy@yandex.ru, behind a `mailto:`. Both are unobfuscated, present in the server-rendered HTML, and therefore trivially harvested by any scraper — the phone number in particular invites SMS spam, cold-call recruiting and, more seriously, is a standard input for SIM-swap and social-engineering attacks; a Telegram handle already covers the same 'reach me instantly' need without that exposure. Also public by intent: full real name (the personal brand and the domain), the hackathon city (St Petersburg, from the achievement claim), and the country (Russia, via the GitHub profile). Not exposed: no home or postal address, no date of birth, no employer, no ID or document numbers, no photograph of the owner anywhere on the site (there are zero `` elements), and no scans or certificates. Third-party PII: none is published on the site — his two hackathon teammates are named only in the linked VK post, i.e. by the organiser rather than by him, so the site does not itself expose anyone else's data. Visitor-side privacy is, by contrast, exemplary and worth noting as the counterweight: no analytics, no tracking pixel, no cookie banner, no third-party script of any kind, and no forms — the site collects nothing from the people who read it. Net recommendation if this pattern were borrowed: keep the email and Telegram, drop the phone number.
